title: Spatial Discretization Error for Quantum Chemistry Simulation
abstract: Nonrelativistic quantum chemistry is based on the Schrödinger equation in continuous, unbounded space. Computational approaches on classical and quantum computers often truncate the spatial domain and introduce a finite-dimensional basis, reducing the continuum problem to a finite-dimensional one. There is therefore a fundamental question: to what extent does this approximation capture the original continuum problem? In this work, we develop a general Sobolev-Galerkin framework for estimating spatial discretization errors in quantum simulation with unbounded Hamiltonians. We apply this framework to many-body Coulomb systems and establish both periodization and Galerkin error estimates for wave-function dynamics and ground-state energies. For dynamics, the finite-basis projection error of the exact wave function does not capture the full basis-discretization error: an additional dynamical projection error enters our bound at a different rate, and we introduce an inner-product argument to control this contribution. Interestingly, the spatial convergence rates for wave-function dynamics and ground-state energies differ quantitatively. For ground-state energies, we establish a sharp $M^{-1}$ convergence rate at fixed cell size, where $M$ is the number of one-particle basis functions. We also show that a uniform $M^{-1}$ convergence rate is impossible for the corresponding real-time wave-function error with general $H^2$ initial data. The analysis relies on many-body Sobolev estimates with explicit polynomial dependence on system size. Combining these estimates with state-of-the-art quantum algorithms, we obtain, to our knowledge, the first rigorous end-to-end complexity bounds for quantum simulation of molecular and electronic dynamics with all spatial errors explicitly controlled. The number of basis functions is determined directly from the continuum problem, without regularization.
summary: This paper develops a rigorous Sobolev-Galerkin framework to quantify spatial discretization errors when simulating quantum chemistry problems involving unbounded Hamiltonians. By analyzing the error sources for both ground-state energies and real-time dynamics, the authors establish sharp convergence rates and provide the first comprehensive complexity bounds for quantum simulation algorithms. This is vital for building reliable quantum computers for molecular physics.
main_problem: The paper develops a rigorous framework to estimate the spatial discretization errors inherent in approximating continuum quantum problems governed by the Schrödinger equation in unbounded space.
main_result: It establishes sharp convergence rates for ground-state energies ($M^{-1}$) and provides the first rigorous end-to-end complexity bounds for quantum simulation of molecular dynamics with all spatial errors explicitly controlled.
method: The core method is a general Sobolev-Galerkin framework applied to error estimation, decomposing the total error into finite-basis projection and dynamical projection components.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on many-body Coulomb systems, which are central to nonrelativistic quantum chemistry and electronic structure calculations. The Hamiltonian involves the full-space Coulomb interaction.
key_observables: Spatial discretization errors for wave-function dynamics and ground-state energies; convergence rates ($M^{-1}$ for ground state, $4/3$-order for dynamics).
important_parameters: The number of one-particle basis functions ($M$); the nature of the Coulomb singularity; the required regularity of the initial wave function ($H^2$ data).
main_assumptions: The analysis requires controlling errors from both the finite computational domain (periodization) and the finite basis set, explicitly handling the singular, long-ranged Coulomb interaction.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of approximating continuum quantum systems, develops the Sobolev-Galerkin framework, applies it to Coulomb systems, derives separate error bounds for dynamics and ground states, and concludes with complexity bounds for quantum algorithms.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial theoretical rigor for implementing quantum simulations of molecular and electronic structure, directly addressing the systematic errors that plague current numerical and quantum computational approaches.
